opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I never thought about it that much. People sometimes assume the ACM class was this intensely competitive environment where everyone was fighting over rankings, and there was some of that, of course. Everyone there was very talented, and you could feel the pressure. But for me, rank was never really the goal.

What I cared about more was whether I was learning something I found interesting. In the first year or two I was probably like everyone else: you take the courses, do the assignments, try to do well on exams. Later I realized grades are a very narrow measure. Being first or second doesn't tell you much about whether you'll do good research, or whether you'll find a problem you really want to spend years on.

The most valuable thing about the ACM class wasn't the ranking. It was the people around you and the exposure. You had classmates who were brilliant in different ways. Some were incredibly good at programming contests, some at math, some just had very original ideas. Being in that environment pushes you, but in a healthy way. You see what's possible.

So my attitude was roughly this: do well enough that it doesn't limit your options, and put the rest of your energy into the things that actually excite you. For me, that turned out to be getting into a lab early and doing real research, even if it was very naive at the beginning. That mattered much more to where I ended up than whether I was first or tenth in the class.

r001.rationale: The response mentions classmates with different strengths, but it does not say that diverse evaluation standards made it difficult to identify who ranked first or second.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I never really thought about it that way. In the ACM class at Shanghai Jiao Tong, everyone around you is extremely strong, so if you spend your energy worrying about whether you're first or second, you'll burn out very quickly. What I cared more about was whether I was actually learning something, whether I understood the problem in front of me.

I think rankings are a bit of an illusion anyway. In a class like that, the difference between first and fifth is often just noise, it depends on which exam, which semester, who happened to be interested in which course. What stays with you long term isn't the number, it's the habits you build and the people you work with. A lot of my classmates from that time are now doing very impressive things, and nobody remembers who had the higher GPA.

If anything, I'd say the ACM class taught me to be comfortable not being the best in the room. That turned out to be really important later, in grad school and in research, because research is exactly a situation where you're constantly facing things you don't know and people who know more than you. You have to be okay with that, and even enjoy it. So I'd tell students: don't optimize for the ranking, optimize for curiosity. The ranking takes care of itself, or it doesn't, and either way it's fine.

r001.rationale: The response calls rankings noisy and dependent on the exam, semester, and course interests, but does not explain that diverse evaluation standards made it difficult to identify who ranked first or second.

astra-6.text: At the time, I cared a lot about grades. When you’re surrounded by strong classmates, it’s natural to compare yourself with them and want to be first or second. It gives you a clear target. But looking back, I think the more important question is what you’re actually learning and what interests you. In research, there isn’t a fixed exam where someone already knows the answer. You have to decide which questions are worth asking. That requires a different mindset from trying to rank at the top of a class.
